newsitem.title: CHINA: China premier says state firms top 1996 problem.
newsitem.headline: China premier says state firms top 1996 problem.

text.p: The mounting losses of state-owned enterprises are among the most serious problems troubling China's economy in a year when it is doing quite well overall, Premier Li Peng told a cabinet meeting.

"Viewing the country as a whole, the situation was good during the first half of the year, but there were still quite a few problems," the People's Daily on Wednesday quoted Li as telling a meeting of the State Council, or cabinet, on Tuesday.
Summing up China's situation in the first half of the year and outlining major tasks for the rest of 1996, Li cited the difficulties of state enterprises as among the major problems.
Economic efficiency in state firms had declined and some were experiencing greater difficulties in both production and management, he said.
The total profit of state industrial enterprises had declined, he said without giving details.
Money-losing enterprises remained stuck in the red, while the number of firms that had stopped production had continued to rise in 1996, Li said.

China's state sector reported a net loss of 3.0 billion yuan ($361 million) in the first quarter of this year, the first such deficit since paramount leader Deng Xiaoping launched his market reforms in 1979.

Officials say the losses eased in the second quarter to put the state sector back in the black overall, but 43 percent of China's estimated 100,000 state firms are chronically in the red and another 30 percent are reporting losses.

Many state firms had been unable to adjust output to produce goods that could find a market, putting them at a disadvantage in the face of strong domestic and international competition, Premier Li said in his report to the cabinet meeting.

He attributed the problems of lumbering state enterprises to their failure to improve management methods, output of products that no one wants to buy and the burdens of a system that still requires state firms to provide cradle-to-grave welfare and virtual jobs-for-life to all employees and their dependents.
Top economic officials have called repeatedly on state firms to boost management and efficiency, saying they cannot continue to rely on easy loans from state-owned banks.

However, Beijing has shown signs of easing a three-year-old credit squeeze in recent months, cutting interest rates twice and allowing loans to a few designated state firms as enterprise managers have begged for credit to help them out of their difficulties and to pay wages.

Li said China must work over the next few months to ensure a good harvest this year. He told regional officials to prepare in advance to make grain purchases and to pay farmers in cash, to give them incentive to produce, instead of in unpopular IOUs.
China has said it hopes for a 480 million tonne grain harvest, up from last year's recrod 465 million tonnes.
Li also stressed the need to control inflation and to maintain a tight monetary policy.

China's retail price inflation was a year-on-year 5.8 percent in August and central bank governor Dai Xianglong said on Tuesday he expected inflation for the year to be about 7.0 percent, below a government target of 10 percent.
Li also said fixed asset investment must not be allowed to race out of control, with key construction projects to be favoured in poorer and more backward central and western regions.
